intro.html: Sooner or later, everyone gives in. These words tell how: by following a rule, by stepping aside, by softening after saying no, by quietly going along, by surrendering completely, or by bowing far too low.

Following a rule or request: comply, accede (agree). Giving way: yield, submit, relent (soften after refusing), succumb (give in to pressure or temptation). Giving something up: concession. Going along: acquiesce (quietly, often unwillingly). Surrendering: capitulate. Too humble: kowtow.

words.def: to do what is asked, ordered or required
words.ex: All visitors must {comply} with the museum’s no-flash rule.
words.ctx: When the lifeguard blew her whistle and waved everyone out of the water, the swimmers {complied} at once, though a few grumbled as they climbed out.
words.etym: From Italian complire, “to fulfill,” from Latin complere, “to fill up.”

mn.cue: COM-PLY: COME and PLAY by the rules
mn.text: The sign on the door says SHOES OFF, so Kai sits down and takes off his sneakers before he comes in to play. He {complies}.

scene.alt: A boy kneels to take off his sneakers beside a sign that says Shoes Off.

words.def: to give way to pressure, to another person or to traffic
words.ex: Drivers must {yield} to people in the crosswalk.
words.ctx: For an hour the rusty gate held firm, but at last it {yielded} to the farmer’s shoulder and creaked open.
words.etym: From Old English gieldan, “to pay, to give back.”
words.note: Yield also means to produce: the orchard yielded a thousand bushels of fruit.

mn.text: Dev stops his bike and waits while a line of ducks waddles across the path. He {yields} to the ducks.

scene.alt: A teen stops his bike to let a line of ducks cross the path beside a Yield sign.

words.def: to give in to someone’s authority or control
words.ex: The players {submitted} to the referee’s decision without another word.
words.ctx: After a long tug-of-war over bath time, the puppy finally {submitted}, standing still and dripping while Lila scrubbed behind his ears.
words.etym: From Latin submittere, “to lower, to put under”: sub (under) + mittere (to send, to let go).
words.note: Submit also means to hand something in: to submit an essay.

mn.cue: SUB-MIT: gives in and goes UNDER the suds
mn.text: After a long struggle, the muddy puppy gives up and sits still in the tub of suds. He {submits} to his bath.

scene.alt: A soapy puppy sits glumly in a tub of water, giving in to a bath, while a girl laughs.

words.def: to become less strict or severe; to give in after refusing
words.ex: Mom finally {relented} and let us stay up to watch the meteor shower.
words.ctx: For weeks the coach refused to change the practice time, but when every family signed a letter asking her to, she {relented} and moved it to after dinner.
words.etym: From Medieval Latin relentare, “to soften,” from Latin lentus, “soft, bending.”

mn.text: Ivy begs to borrow her big sister’s bike. Maya says no, no and no again, then sighs and lends it after all. Maya {relents}.

scene.alt: A teen sighs and lends her bike to her delighted little sister.

words.def: to give in to pressure, temptation or force
words.ex: After an hour of staring at the cake, Jonah {succumbed} and ate a slice.
words.ctx: The old oak had survived a hundred storms, but in last night’s wind it finally {succumbed}, crashing down across the empty road.
words.etym: From Latin succumbere, “to sink down under”: sub (under) + cumbere (to lie down).

mn.cue: suc-CRUMB: gives in to the CRUMB
mn.text: Jonah promised himself no sweets, but the chocolate cake smells so good. He {succumbs} and takes a big bite.

labels.text: suc-CUMB: gives IN to the crumb

scene.alt: A teen gives in and takes a bite of chocolate cake despite his No Sweets sign.

words.def: something given up or allowed in order to reach an agreement
words.ex: As a {concession}, the coach let the team choose the music for practice.
words.ctx: Neither side would budge until the landlord made a {concession}: she would fix the leaky roof if the tenants agreed to a slightly higher rent.
words.etym: From Latin concessio, from concedere, “to give way”: con (thoroughly) + cedere (to yield).
words.note: A concession stand sells snacks at a game; its owner has been granted, or conceded, the right to sell there.

mn.cue: a CONE-cession: give a CONE to make a deal
mn.text: Pip and Zoe both want the swing. Pip hands Zoe his ice cream cone, and she lets him swing first. The cone is his {concession}.

labels.text: a CONE-CESSION: a give-up for a deal

scene.alt: A boy offers his ice cream cone to a girl so that he can have the swing first.

words.def: to accept or agree quietly, without protest, often unwillingly
words.ex: Too tired to argue, Grandpa {acquiesced} to watching the cartoon movie one more time.
words.ctx: Rosa had wanted pizza, but when the rest of the family voted for soup, she {acquiesced} with a small sigh and set the table without another word.
words.etym: From Latin acquiescere, “to rest, to be at peace with”: ad (to) + quiescere (to be quiet).
words.note: Acquiesce means quiet acceptance, often with a sigh, not eager agreement.

mn.text: The family votes for soup instead of pizza. Rosa sighs, says nothing and quietly sets out the bowls: she {acquiesces}.

scene.alt: A teen quietly carries a soup bowl while her father and little brother cheer for soup.

words.def: to surrender or give in completely
words.ex: After a long siege, the castle finally {capitulated}.
words.ctx: The twins held out against bedtime for nearly an hour, bargaining and pleading, but at last they {capitulated} and climbed into bed.
words.etym: From Medieval Latin capitulare, “to draw up terms under headings,” from capitulum, “a chapter, a little head”; to capitulate was first to agree to terms of surrender.

mn.cue: CAP-itulate: off comes the CAP, up goes the white flag
mn.text: King Gus takes off his crown, raises both hands and waves a white flag from the castle: “We give up!” He {capitulates}.

scene.alt: A king with his crown on the ground raises his hands in surrender as a white flag flies from the castle.

words.def: to agree to a request or demand
words.ex: The principal {acceded} to the students’ request for a longer lunch.
words.ctx: At first the town council refused, but after hundreds of letters it {acceded} to the neighbors’ demand and put a stop sign at the busy corner.
words.etym: From Latin accedere, “to come near, to agree”: ad (to) + cedere (to go, to yield).

mn.cue: ac-SEED: says YES to more SEEDS
mn.text: The birds line up and squawk for more seeds, and Granny Mae says yes, tossing out another handful. She {accedes} to their demand.

scene.alt: A grandmother on a bench tosses more seeds to a row of squawking birds.

words.def: to act too humbly and obediently in order to please someone powerful
words.ex: The new player refused to {kowtow} to the bossy team captain.
words.ctx: Instead of standing up for her own idea, Rosa’s partner {kowtowed} to the loudest kid in the group, agreeing with every word he said.
words.etym: From Chinese kòutóu, “knock the head,” an old custom of kneeling and touching the forehead to the ground before a ruler.

mn.cue: KOW-TOW: bow down to your TOES
mn.text: Whatever bossy Pip in the paper crown says, Sami bows down to his toes: “Yes, boss! Anything, boss!” Sami {kowtows}.

labels.text: KOW-TOW: bow LOW to the boss

scene.alt: A boy bows low before a bossy boy wearing a paper crown and standing on a crate.

after.html: Two traps. Accede (agree) is not exceed (go beyond): the council acceded to our request, and the cost did not exceed our budget. And acquiesce means quiet acceptance, often with a sigh, not eager agreement. Notice, too, that kowtow is a criticism: it means being too humble, not simply polite.

opts.s: The twins begged for a puppy for a whole year before Dad finally {relented}.
opts.why: Giving in after refusing for a long time is relenting.

items.q: After a month of letters, the town council ______ to the students’ request for a bike rack. Which word fits?
items.why: To accede is to agree to a request. Exceed means to go beyond, which makes no sense here.

items.q: True or false: to acquiesce is to agree eagerly and excitedly.
items.why: False. Acquiesce means to go along quietly, without protest, often unwillingly.

items.q: In “The garden yielded twenty pounds of tomatoes,” yielded means…
items.why: Yield has two senses: to give way, and to produce. A garden that yields tomatoes produces them.
Sub (under) + cumbere (to lie down): to succumb is to sink under pressure.

items.q: Type the noun for something given up or allowed in order to reach an agreement.
items.why: A concession is what one side gives up to make a deal.
